deep.reconstruction:
The page is a research programme of three problems. It contains no derivations. Hilbert's notebook 600:1 is a running list of 'Probleme', and the previous and next pages are of the same kind.

(1) Reciprocity laws proved geometrically. Hilbert wants to prove the biquadratic and higher (l-th power) reciprocity laws 'geometrically', as the quadratic law can be proved. That means generalising Gauss's proof, citing 'Gauss, höhere Arithmetik S. 457'. This is H. Maser's German edition, 'Carl Friedrich Gauss' Untersuchungen über höhere Arithmetik' (1889). The Disquisitiones fill roughly its first 450 pages, so p. 457 is plausibly where the 'Theorematis arithmetici demonstratio nova' (1808) begins. That is Gauss's third proof, via Gauss's lemma (my identification).

In modern form that proof runs as follows (my reconstruction):
- Gauss's lemma gives (q/p) = (-1)^{mu}.
- Here mu = sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} floor(kq/p) mod 2, for odd q.
- Counting lattice points in the rectangle 0 < x < p/2, 0 < y < q/2, split by the diagonal py = qx, gives sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2} floor(kq/p) + sum_{k=1}^{(q-1)/2} floor(kp/q) = (p-1)/2 * (q-1)/2.
- Hence (p/q)(q/p) = (-1)^{(p-1)(q-1)/4}.
Eisenstein made this argument 'geometric'. Hilbert asks for an analogue for quartic and higher residue symbols, presumably via lattice-point counting in Z[i], Z[zeta_l], etc.

(2) 'Ueber die Endlichkeit beliebiger voller Formensysteme (oder Funktionensysteme)'.
- Definition: a 'full system of forms' is a set S of forms in x_1,...,x_n such that every algebraic function of arbitrary forms of S which is rational in x_1,...,x_n again belongs to S. In modern terms, S is a graded k-subalgebra of k[x_1..x_n] that is algebraically closed in k[x] (relatively algebraically closed). That is, f in k[x] algebraic over S implies f in S.
- Conjecture: such a system is finitely generated.
- Proposed method: reduce to Kronecker's theorem on the finiteness of the integral algebraic quantities of a domain of rationality. That theorem is the existence of a finite integral basis, Kronecker's Grundzüge 1882.
- Intended application: invariant theory for arbitrary linear substitutions (arbitrary groups). For connected groups the invariant ring is algebraically closed in k[x], so it is a 'full system'.
- Further claim: all invariants are expressible integrally, with integer coefficients, in finitely many of them. This connects to the last problem on the previous page (integer invariants of an integral substitution).
- The term 'volles System' recurs in Hilbert's 1893 Math. Ann. paper 'Über die vollen Invariantensysteme'. The problem is a direct precursor of Hilbert's 14th Paris problem (1900).

(3) Kummer's reciprocity law beyond cyclotomic fields. Hilbert wants to generalise Kummer's general reciprocity law (for l-th powers in Q(zeta_l)) from cyclotomic fields to all Galois fields, 'perhaps first abelian'. The footnote cites Crelle's Journal vol. 100 (1887). This is a precursor of Hilbert's 9th problem and of his later reciprocity programme (Zahlbericht 1897, 'relativ-quadratische Zahlkörper' 1899). The citations fix a date of 1889 or later.
errors: The finiteness conjecture for arbitrary 'full systems' is false in general. Nagata (1959) gave a counterexample: the invariant ring of a connected unipotent group action, which is algebraically closed in k[x], is not finitely generated. So this programme cannot succeed in the stated generality, and no reduction to Kronecker's finite integral basis theorem can exist. Zariski (1954) proved finiteness only in transcendence degree <= 2.

The integer-coefficient ('ganzzahlig') finiteness for invariants of arbitrary integral linear substitutions likewise fails in general, because it inherits Nagata-type counterexamples. It holds for finite groups and for reductive groups over Z by later results (e.g. Seshadri 1977).

The reduction to Kronecker's theorem is only sketched. Kronecker's integral-basis finiteness concerns modules over a finitely generated base, whereas here the base ring itself is unknown. This is the gap that is the essential difficulty.

The geometric proof of higher reciprocity laws was never achieved in the naive lattice-point form. Higher laws were proved through Kummer/Hilbert norm-residue symbols and class field theory (Takagi, Artin 1927).

results.what: Programme: prove biquadratic and higher reciprocity laws by generalising Gauss's third (lattice-point / Gauss-lemma) proof geometrically
results.modern_name: Gauss's lemma / Eisenstein lattice-point proof of quadratic reciprocity; geometric proofs of higher reciprocity
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss 1808, Eisenstein 1844 (geometric form); higher laws: Eisenstein, Kummer, Hilbert, Furtwängler, Artin

results.what: Definition of 'full systems of forms' (subalgebras of k[x] algebraically closed in k[x]) and conjecture of their finite generation, to be reduced to Kronecker's integral-basis theorem and applied to invariants of arbitrary linear groups, including integer coefficients
results.modern_name: Hilbert's 14th problem (finite generation of k[x] ∩ L / invariant rings); refuted by Nagata's counterexample
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert 1900 (14th problem), with antecedents in Hilbert 1890/1893; Zariski 1954; Nagata 1959

results.what: Programme: extend Kummer's general reciprocity law from cyclotomic fields to all abelian, then all Galois, number fields

deep.surprise_reason: The ideas behind Hilbert's 14th and 9th Paris problems are well known to be his. Here they appear around 1889-1891 as private research goals: the general finiteness of 'full systems' via Kronecker, with an integer-coefficient variant, and reciprocity for all Galois fields. That is a notable early documentation, but not a new result; Hilbert used 'volles System' publicly in 1893.

checkable.asserts: Quadratic reciprocity law, the model case Hilbert wants to generalise
